source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Game of 24
finding: A breadth-limited best-first style search over thoughts, with the model scoring each state, beats plain and sampled chain of thought by a wide margin.
numbers: GPT-4, 100 games. IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. Best-of-100 CoT reaches 49%. About 60% of CoT samples already fail after the first step.
quote: Around 60% of CoT samples already failed after generating the first step
limits: Model-scored heuristic (sure/maybe/impossible), no admissibility guarantee. One task with tiny depth (3 steps). GPT-4 only in main run.
agent_relevance: Ranking children at S6 with a cheap value call and keeping b candidates beats resampling at similar token cost; failure is early, so rank early.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: crosswords and ablations
finding: On a deeper task (5x5 mini crosswords) search with a model heuristic plus pruning plus backtracking lifts results; removing pruning or backtracking costs a lot.
numbers: IO 38.7 letter / 14 word / 0 games; CoT 40.6 / 15.6 / 1; ToT 78 / 60 / 4 of 20 games. With oracle best state 82.4 / 67.5 / 35. Ablate prune: 65.4 / 41.5 / 5. Ablate backtrack: 54.6 / 20 / 5.
limits: Heuristic is the model judging its own thoughts, so errors in the judge cap results (oracle best state shows large headroom). 20 test games only.
agent_relevance: Heuristic quality is the bottleneck: the gap to the oracle state-picker is the headroom for a better S6 ranker (code check beats model self-rating).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: cost and model strength (appendix B)
finding: Search costs about as many tokens as 100 chain-of-thought trials but wins; a weaker model works much worse as generator or judge.
numbers: Game of 24: ToT 5.5k completion tokens, close to 100 CoT trials (6.7k tokens). GPT-3.5 with ToT 19% vs GPT-4 74%; GPT-4 generating with GPT-3.5 judging 64%. Creative writing ToT about 5x tokens and cost.
limits: Prices are 2023 API prices. Only one task for the model comparison.
agent_relevance: Judge strength matters about as much as generator strength; do not downgrade the ranker to save tokens without a test (G7).

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Searchformer
finding: A transformer trained on A* execution traces (not only final plans) plans better than one trained on plans alone, and after bootstrapping it uses fewer search steps than the A* that taught it.
numbers: Sokoban, 200 unseen tasks: solution-only 45M model 90.3% solved / 86.8% optimal; search-augmented 92.5 / 90.8; Searchformer 95.5-96.0 solved, 93.4-93.7 optimal, up to 26.8% fewer search steps than the A* teacher. Claim: 5-10x smaller model and 10x smaller data than solution-only baselines.
limits: Synthetic mazes and Sokoban, trained from scratch, not a general LLM. Heuristic fixed (Manhattan / box matching) in the teacher.
agent_relevance: Showing the search trace helps; supports writing the open set and rankings out explicitly instead of jumping to an answer. Not a prompting result.

source: Gandhi et al. (2024) Stream of Search
finding: Training a language model on flattened search traces (including mistakes and backtracking) beats training on optimal paths only; later self-improvement can exceed the heuristic solvers that made the data.
numbers: Countdown. SoS model 51.27% on held-out inputs vs 25.73% for optimal-path model (about +25 points). After APA/STaR finetuning solves about 36% of previously unsolved problems and about 4% of problems no heuristic solver solved. SoS data: 285,501 (57.1%) correct trajectories.
limits: Small model pretrained from scratch on one task. Not prompting.
agent_relevance: Seeing failed branches helps; hints that a log of rejected children (open/closed set) is useful context, but only shown by training.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning via Planning (RAP)
finding: MCTS where the LLM is also the world model (predicts next state) lifts a small model far above chain of thought on block-stacking.
numbers: Blocksworld, LLaMA-33B: CoT 0.17/0.02/0.00 (2/4/6 steps); RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42; GPT-4 CoT 0.50/0.63/0.40. Llama-2 70B full Blocksworld Easy: CoT 0.08 overall vs RAP(10) 0.65; Hard: 0.05 vs 0.51. GSM8K 48.8% RAP. PrOntoQA proof accuracy 78.8% vs CoT 64.8%.
limits: Uses MCTS, not A*; rewards include model self-evaluation. At 6 steps LLaMA-33B RAP still only 26-42%. Tests are 4-5 block cases.
agent_relevance: Explicit state tracking plus search beats reading history; at S6, feed the current state only, not the history, when scoring.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) LATS
finding: MCTS with model value plus reflection beats ToT, RAP and Reflexion in code and QA, and ablations show the model heuristic and the search algorithm both matter.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1: GPT-4 base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7; GPT-3.5 LATS 83.8 vs ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, Reflexion 68.1. MBPP GPT-3.5: ToT 65.8, RAP 71.4, LATS 81.1. HotPotQA EM ablation: LATS 0.63, no reflection 0.58, DFS 0.42, no LM heuristic 0.37; ToT 0.39; RAP 0.54. Uses 8 iterations, 5 samples per expansion.
limits: Argues MCTS is more principled than A* or DFS variants but tests only a DFS variant; costs more calls than ReAct. Needs a revertible environment.
agent_relevance: Dropping the model-scored heuristic costs about 26 points of EM on HotPotQA, so ranking matters more than the loop shape.

source: Koh et al. (2024/2026) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Best-first search loosely inspired by A*, with a model value function (average of 20 reasoning paths) and environment rollback, lifts web agents.
numbers: VisualWebArena (910 tasks): GPT-4o+SoM 18.9% -> 26.4% (+39.7% relative); Llama-3-70B 7.6 -> 16.7%. WebArena (812 tasks): GPT-4o 15.0 -> 19.2% (+28.0%); Llama-3-70B 7.6 -> 10.1%.
limits: Other WebArena agents without search (AgentOccam 43.1%, 45.7% with judge) score far higher, so search is not the only lever. Needs reversible states; up to 20x more model calls.
agent_relevance: Best-first beats greedy for agents at a stated budget; relative gains are modest when the heuristic is a model self-score.

source: Koh et al. (2024/2026) Tree Search: budget, depth, value function
finding: More node expansions and bigger trees help steadily; wider and deeper both needed.
limits: Single-run numbers on 200 tasks; no error bars in the text I read. Value function is a model and can reward wrong states.
agent_relevance: Gives a scaling curve: 5 expansions already gets about 60% of the gain, so a small S6 budget is a defensible default.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Q*: A* with a learned Q-value heuristic
finding: Treats multi-step reasoning as A*: f = accumulated utility + a learned Q-value heuristic h, expanding the highest f node.
numbers: GSM8K Llama-2-7b MetaMath base 74.5%; PPO(QVM) 80.8%; Q* reported to beat Best-of-N. MATH: DeepSeek-Math-7b base 50.8%, with Q* 55.4%. MBPP: CodeQwen1.5-7b-Chat 77.0% with Q*. (Several table cells for Q* on GSM8K lost in text extraction.)
limits: Preprint; heuristic needs a trained Q-value model per task and offline data; not admissible or consistent, no guarantee. Gains over Best-of-N are a few points.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM work to A* proper. A learned h beats model self-rating but needs training, which a no-training scaffold cannot do.

source: Feng et al. (2024) AlphaZero-like Tree Search (TS-LLM)
finding: A learned value function beats prompting the LLM to score its own thoughts, in every pairing tested.
numbers: Game24 ToT-BFS Path@1: prompt-based value with GPT-3.5 policy 15.5% vs learned value 19.1%; LLaMA-SFT policy: prompt value LLaMA 9.2, GPT-3.5 21.0, learned 64.8 (task rows as extracted). GSM8K: GPT-3.5 policy/ToT 72.7; LLaMA-SFT 37.4 / 45.8 / 52.5 with learned value. Authors say prompt self-evaluation is not reliable, citing Huang et al. 2023 and Stechly et al. 2023.
limits: Needs training of a value network. Task-to-row mapping in the extracted table is partly uncertain.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G5: do not trust the model to rank its own branches; use code checks or a separate scorer.

source: Zhao et al. (2023) LLM-MCTS
finding: Using an LLM as a commonsense prior (policy heuristic) inside MCTS beats using the LLM policy alone on household rearrangement.
numbers: VirtualHome, success rate %: UCT without LLM 0.0 on every task type. Seen scenes: GPT3.5 policy simple 83.4, GPT3.5-MCTS 91.4. Unseen scenes: GPT3.5 policy 74.3 / 43.3, GPT3.5-MCTS 82.9 / 71.9 (column mapping partly uncertain).
limits: Table text garbled in extraction; trends are reliable, exact column mapping is not. MCTS not A*.
agent_relevance: Blind search with no heuristic gets 0%: the heuristic is what makes search affordable; the model works as a prior.

source: Lin et al. (2023) LLM A*: human-in-the-loop A*
finding: GPT-3.5 gives A* waypoints and a direction prior; paths are close to A* with fewer expanded nodes, but longer and less smooth.
numbers: 3 grid maps, mean of 3 runs. Path length: A* 27/24/31; LLM A* 34/27.67/37.33; greedy LLM 48.67/41.67/45.67; PPO 37.33/29/38. Nodes expanded: A* 372/145/210; LLM A* 352/133/197.67; greedy LLM 100.67/74/103.67.
limits: Tiny maps, 3 runs, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, human feedback inside the loop. Not optimal. Greedy variant worst in path length.
agent_relevance: Guided search saves little over A* (352 vs 372 nodes) while greedy ranking saves much but loses quality: trade-off between greedy and weighted ranking.

source: Correa, Pereira, Seipp (2025) Classical planning with LLM-generated heuristics
finding: Ask the LLM once per domain for several Python heuristic functions, pick the best on training tasks, then run greedy best-first search. Search stays sound; the LLM only supplies h.
numbers: 8 IPC-style domains, 720 test tasks (larger than training). Solved: DeepSeek R1 heuristics 373, DeepSeek V3 343, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking 305, hFF (Pyperplan) 234, blind h0 120, best end-to-end LLM planning 174. Generation cost $0.25 (V3) and $6.12 (R1) total. Going from 1 to 5 sampled heuristics gave the biggest coverage gain.
limits: Python planner vs C++ baselines elsewhere. R1 distill 14B heuristics fell below hFF. hFF beats the LLM heuristic in Floortile. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning ones.
agent_relevance: Key transfer: use the model to write the ranking function once, check it in code on training cases, keep search sound. Sample about 5 candidates and select by code.

source: Correa, Pereira, Seipp (2025): informedness check
finding: The generated heuristics are sometimes more informed than hFF (fewer expansions) and sometimes just cheaper to compute.
numbers: R1 heuristics expand fewer states than hFF in Blocksworld, Spanner, Transport, most Childsnack; hFF better in Floortile, Rovers, Sokoban. In Rovers and Sokoban R1 solves as many or more despite being less informed, because it is faster per node.
limits: Evaluated with GBFS only.
agent_relevance: Cost per ranking call matters as much as quality; a cheap code scorer can beat a better but slower one.

source: Tuisov, Vernik, Shleyfman (2025/2026) Successor-generator planning with LLM heuristics
finding: LLM writes a problem-specific heuristic from a successor generator, goal test and initial state, then GBFS runs without more LLM calls.
numbers: 400 tasks in 20 domains: blind BFS 39, ENHSP hmd 175, best portfolio of domain-independent heuristics 234. LLM-heuristic configurations from GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, Claude Sonnet 4.5 (first-compile, until-success, self-portfolio of 10) range about 188 to 281; best from GPT-5.1 with high reasoning. GPT-4.1 best when generation time and cost counted.
limits: Table layout garbled in my text extraction, so per-column assignment of totals is uncertain; the range is reliable. Compilation errors are common. Includes numeric domains.
agent_relevance: Confirms the 2025 result with newer models; retrying until a heuristic compiles and a portfolio of 10 raises coverage. Cheap models are enough on a cost-adjusted view.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench / On the planning abilities of LLMs
finding: LLMs alone almost never produce valid plans in IPC-style domains; human baselines are far higher.
numbers: About 3% of plans executable and goal-reaching on average (abstract); human baseline 78% for plan generation, 70% for optimal planning. GPT-3 Blocksworld plan generation 6/600 (1%); Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%). Mystery Blocksworld: 0/600 for GPT-3, 8/600 (1.3%) Instruct-GPT3. A later version of the paper reports about 12% for GPT-4.
limits: Early-2023 models. Human baseline called preliminary. Obfuscated names remove surface cues, so scores drop to near 0.
agent_relevance: The model without search is a poor planner; the scaffold must supply the search and the check.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs still can't plan; can LRMs? (o1 on PlanBench)
finding: o1 sharply improves on Blocksworld but not on obfuscated or long problems; it can also claim to solve unsolvable ones.
numbers: 600 instances: o1-preview 97.8% Blocksworld, 52.8% Mystery Blocksworld, 37.3% Randomized Mystery; best LLaMA 3.1 405B 62.6% on regular Blocksworld; GPT-4 about 10% on Mystery with translation. 110 long instances (20-40 steps): o1-preview 23.63%. Fast Downward 100% on all. Unsolvable: only 27% correctly identified as unsolvable in Randomized Mystery.
limits: Preliminary, closed model, token cost and time per instance far above a classical planner.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models close the gap on easy domains only; for long horizons keep an external planner or checker (G3).

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning in LLM-Modulo
finding: Proposes generate-and-test: LLM proposes, external verifiers critique, back-prompt until pass.
numbers: Blocks World: back prompting from the VAL verifier raises performance to 82% within 15 rounds; Logistics to 70%; Mystery Blocks World about 10%; best strategies on TravelPlanner 0.7% (as quoted from prior work).
limits: Position paper; numbers quoted from Valmeekam et al. 2023c and Gundawar et al. 2024. Needs a sound verifier per domain.
agent_relevance: Same shape as our G2/G3: revise only from real verifier output. Obfuscated domains still fail, so a verifier helps only if the model can propose plausible candidates.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: soundness and completeness
finding: Ask the LLM to write the successor function and goal test as code, then run plain BFS/DFS: sound, complete, and only a few LLM calls.
numbers: 24 game 1,362 puzzles, Crossword 20 games, BlocksWorld 502 tasks, PrOntoQA 4,000 questions: 100% accuracy on all, run time seconds (Crossword 5.5 s to 346 s total). ToT reported 75% on Game 24 using about 100 LLM calls; ToT crosswords bounded at 100 expansions = up to 200 calls per game.
limits: Crosswords assume 10 candidate answers per clue are given. Uninformed search only; larger Blocksworld would need a heuristic.
agent_relevance: Calling the model per node is the expensive part. Moving expansion and goal tests into code is the strongest alternative to model ranking at S6.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: cost of per-node LLM calls
finding: Per-node LLM calls make search very costly; a code-based search is far cheaper.
numbers: BlocksWorld (447 4-block and 55 5-block instances): 50,143 expanded and 129,408 generated states; calling GPT-4 on every node would take about 14 days and over $1000 with no correctness guarantee.
limits: Author estimate, not measured.
agent_relevance: Budget guard: count model calls per expansion before choosing a search width.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2025) Chain of Thoughtlessness
finding: Chain-of-thought hints for planning only help if narrowly tailored to the problem class, and they collapse as the problem grows.
numbers: Blocksworld goal stacks of n=3 to 20 blocks, two frontier LLMs: improvement only for very specific prompts; accuracy falls as n grows past the size in the examples; scalable variants of three other domains show the same failure.
limits: Exact accuracies are in figures not captured in text. Simple stacking problems only.
agent_relevance: Generic reasoning prompts do not teach a search algorithm; the loop must run the algorithm.

source: Wang et al. (2024) PlanSearch
finding: Searching over diverse natural-language plans, not code, raises the pass rate; diversity of ideas predicts search gains.
numbers: LiveCodeBench, Claude 3.5 Sonnet: pass@1 no search 41.4%; repeated sampling pass@200 60.6%; PlanSearch pass@200 77.0%. Diversity score (LLM-as-judge) strongly correlates with gains across models and algorithms. Accuracy conditioned on a sketch tends toward 0% or 100%.
limits: Pass@k assumes a perfect selector; real selection is harder.
agent_relevance: Branch diversity matters before ranking: rank among different ideas, not near-duplicates (G4).

source: Aghzal, Plaku, Yao (2023/2025) Can LLMs be good path planners? (PPNL)
finding: GPT-4 with ReAct (environment feedback) is the best prompt on grid path planning; plain CoT is weaker on many obstacles and far goals.
numbers: ReAct 96.1% success, gap of only 2% between overall and the 4-or-more-obstacle subset. CoT falls 7% on environments with 4+ obstacles and fails on the 6-11 out-of-distribution set. Failed ReAct cases end on average 5.26 steps from the goal. Fine-tuned BART/T5 do well in distribution but fail on larger grids.
limits: Authors blame the time dimension (long horizon), not spatial reasoning. Other metrics in the table not fully checked.
agent_relevance: Environment feedback beats pure reasoning for path tasks; supports the revise-from-output rule.

source: Hart, Nilsson, Raphael (1968) A formal basis for A*
finding: A* with an admissible heuristic (never overestimates) returns an optimal path; consistent heuristics never reopen nodes.
numbers: Theory result, no sample.
limits: Not opened this session; stated from background knowledge. Admissibility needs exact cost bounds; LLM scores cannot be admissible by construction.
agent_relevance: LLM heuristic scores are never admissible; keep a quick exact check where possible.
